learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: A person prefers a guaranteed payment to a gamble with the same average cash payment. Why is this compatible with expected-utility theory?
option_A: The probabilities of the gamble must have been calculated incorrectly.
option_B: The utilities of the risky outcomes need not average to the utility of the guaranteed payment.
option_C: Expected-utility theory always gives zero weight to possible gains.
option_D: Monetary averages determine all preferences regardless of outcome utilities.
rationale: Expected utility averages utilities of outcomes, rather than monetary payoffs alone.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: A lottery delivers utility 9 with probability 0.25 and utility 1 otherwise. What is its expected utility?
option_A: 3 utility units
option_B: 7 utility units
option_C: 9 utility units
option_D: 1 utility unit
rationale: Multiply 9 by 0.25 and 1 by 0.75, then sum to obtain 3.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: An identical monetary change feels stronger when described as losing money than gaining it from a reference point. Which interpretation fits loss aversion?
option_A: Equal-sized losses and gains may have unequal subjective impacts.
option_B: All people assign exactly twice as much weight to losses.
option_C: Reference points cannot affect the subjective evaluation of money.
option_D: Disliking all risky bets is the definition of loss aversion.
rationale: Loss aversion is a tendency for losses relative to a reference point to loom larger than matching gains.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: Relative to a savings target of 100 monetary units, an outcome leaves 85. How is the outcome classified?
option_A: A loss of 15 relative to the stated target
option_B: A gain of 85 relative to the target
option_C: No change because the outcome is positive
option_D: A loss of 100 regardless of the outcome
rationale: Subtract the reference amount: 85 − 100 = −15.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: A random two-digit number is displayed before a student estimates a population. The number affects estimates. What makes this an anchoring concern?
option_A: The random number is therefore an accurate population statistic.
option_B: Any use of numbers is mathematically incorrect.
option_C: An irrelevant initial number may pull judgments toward itself.
option_D: The student must have been measuring memory availability only.
rationale: Anchoring can bias numerical judgments toward a prior value without informative relevance.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: To test a suspected anchor, a researcher randomly shows high or low irrelevant numbers before the same price-estimation task. What comparison is appropriate?
option_A: Assume the high-anchor group will always be correct.
option_B: Change the product quality only for the high-anchor group.
option_C: Treat the displayed number as the real price without measuring estimates.
option_D: Compare price estimates between the randomly assigned anchor groups.
rationale: Random assignment and a common task isolate the influence of the displayed initial number.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Sunk Cost in a decision-making context.
prompt: An organizer paid a nonrefundable venue deposit. What is the correct role of that payment in choosing between future events?
option_A: The event must proceed simply because the deposit was large.
option_B: The past payment cannot be recovered and should not alone determine the best future option.
option_C: The payment automatically makes future ticket revenue higher.
option_D: Every other future cost becomes irrelevant after a deposit.
rationale: A sunk payment is historical; compare the remaining costs, benefits and alternatives.
source_citation: Arkes and Blumer (1985), The Psychology of Sunk Cost, https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Sunk Cost in a decision-making context.
prompt: A cancelled course already cost 400 irrecoverable units. Restarting would cost 60 more and yield 90 in additional value. What is the forward-looking net value?
option_A: −370 units after treating all historical costs as new
option_B: Exactly 400 units because it was paid earlier
option_C: −60 units because future benefits never count
option_D: +30 units of incremental value
rationale: Future benefit 90 minus future cost 60 equals +30; the sunk 400 does not change this calculation.
source_citation: Arkes and Blumer (1985), The Psychology of Sunk Cost, https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Framing in a decision-making context.
prompt: An intervention is presented as 80% survival rather than 20% mortality, with the same underlying patients. Why might decisions change?
option_A: Survival and mortality automatically describe different medical treatments.
option_B: Different descriptions can emphasize different aspects of identical outcomes.
option_C: The two percentages cannot refer to the same binary outcome.
option_D: A framing effect requires lying about the total number of patients.
rationale: The descriptions are complementary; presentation can influence judgment without changing consequences.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1981), The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7455683

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Framing in a decision-making context.
prompt: In a binary-outcome survey, 36 of 60 participants succeeded. What is the complementary failure percentage?
option_A: 36% failed
option_B: 40% failed
option_C: 60% failed
option_D: 24% failed
rationale: Twenty-four of sixty did not succeed: 24/60 = 0.40.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1981), The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7455683

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Heuristics in a decision-making context.
prompt: After repeatedly watching vivid burglary footage, a resident overestimates the local burglary rate. Which reasoning shortcut is plausible?
option_A: An exact computation using complete local crime records.
option_B: Availability: memorable examples are substituted for representative frequency information.
option_C: A necessary inference that the population rate has doubled.
option_D: Only a decision influenced by already-spent money.
rationale: Salient examples are easily retrieved and can bias judgments about event frequency.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Heuristics in a decision-making context.
prompt: A manager remembers one dramatic product failure but needs to estimate the overall failure rate. What evidence should be used?
option_A: Treat the vivid failure as every recorded trial.
option_B: Ignore the denominator because memorable cases are more informative.
option_C: Use the highest arbitrary number seen in a recent advertisement.
option_D: Count failures and total relevant product trials in a representative dataset.
rationale: A frequency estimate should use an appropriate denominator rather than one memorable incident.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Prospect Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A person evaluates a pay raise in relation to an anticipated salary rather than only total wealth. Which principle is illustrated?
option_A: Objective probabilities must equal one-half in every prospect.
option_B: Reference points can never depend on expectations.
option_C: Prospect theory requires monetary outcomes to be ignored.
option_D: The subjective coding of gains and losses depends on a reference point.
rationale: The same nominal outcome can be coded differently depending on the comparison baseline.
source_citation: Kahneman and Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory, https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Prospect Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A share closes at 45 while the decision maker uses 50 as a reference. What is the reference-relative change?
option_A: A 45-unit gain
option_B: An unchanged outcome
option_C: A 50-unit profit
option_D: A 5-unit loss
rationale: Subtract 50 from 45 to obtain a −5 change.
source_citation: Kahneman and Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory, https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Nudge Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A website preselects an optional reminder but allows immediate cancellation without penalty. Which feature makes this a plausible nudge?
option_A: The alternative option is legally banned.
option_B: The user must pay an unavoidable fee to refuse the reminder.
option_C: The interface guides choice while preserving an accessible alternative.
option_D: All participants are compelled to select the preselected option.
rationale: A reversible default changes choice architecture without eliminating meaningful opt-out.
source_citation: Thaler and Sunstein (2008), Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness, Yale University Press, ISBN 9780300122237

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Nudge Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A savings form preselects an optional contribution rate. What must be verified before describing the design as noncoercive?
option_A: A hidden opt-out button available only after payment.
option_B: A mandatory contribution with no exit path.
option_C: A penalty for every person who changes the default.
option_D: A clear, low-friction ability to change or decline the contribution.
rationale: Preserving meaningful choice requires a transparent and realistically accessible alternative.
source_citation: Thaler and Sunstein (2008), Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness, Yale University Press, ISBN 9780300122237

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: Two people agree on a lottery’s outcome probabilities but rank it differently from a sure amount. Which explanation is compatible with expected utility?
option_A: They can assign different utilities to the same monetary outcomes.
option_B: Agreement on probabilities forces identical preferences over all lotteries.
option_C: A sure payment is never representable by a utility function.
option_D: The larger nominal prize must be preferred by both people.
rationale: Utility functions can represent distinct individual preferences even when objective probabilities agree.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: A game yields utility 10 on one out of four equally likely outcomes and utility 2 on each other outcome. What is the mean utility?
option_A: 8 utility units
option_B: 10 utility units
option_C: 4 utility units
option_D: 2 utility units
rationale: The probability-weighted result is (10 + 2 + 2 + 2)/4 = 4.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: A person wants greater compensation to give up an owned ticket than they would pay to obtain it. What account is consistent with loss aversion?
option_A: Relinquishing the ticket may be evaluated as a loss from the ownership reference state.
option_B: Ownership necessarily changes the ticket’s face value at the box office.
option_C: The observed difference conclusively excludes transaction costs.
option_D: Loss aversion applies only when all possible outcomes are uncertain.
rationale: Treating the owned ticket as the status quo can make relinquishment feel like a loss; alternative explanations remain.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: A worker expected a bonus of 60 units but actually received 75. How is this coded relative to that expectation?
option_A: A gain of 15 relative to the expected bonus
option_B: A loss of 60 relative to the reference
option_C: An unchanged outcome because both amounts are positive
option_D: A gain of exactly 75 beyond expectation
rationale: Use the specified reference expectation: 75 − 60 = +15.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: An applicant sees an arbitrary advertised salary before forming an independent salary estimate. Why might the estimate be biased?
option_A: Any salary mentioned publicly becomes the true market median.
option_B: The visible starting figure can influence the subsequent adjustment.
option_C: The first figure must be chosen using an unbiased representative sample.
option_D: Anchoring requires a complete absence of numerical reasoning.
rationale: A potentially arbitrary initial value can act as a reference that shapes later estimates.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: Two otherwise identical groups estimate a building’s height after seeing different arbitrary reference numbers. How should a possible anchor effect be evaluated?
option_A: Declare the tallest reference number to be the true building height.
option_B: Test whether estimates differ systematically across the assigned reference conditions.
option_C: Conclude that any observed difference proves deliberate deception.
option_D: Replace the task with different buildings for each condition.
rationale: Under randomized assignment, systematic differences between estimates may indicate anchoring, subject to sampling uncertainty.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Sunk Cost in a decision-making context.
prompt: A committee argues that a cancelled prototype must be completed because earlier staff hours were expensive. Which reasoning is sound?
option_A: Previously spent hours guarantee future benefits if more hours are spent.
option_B: Any sunk spending creates a new positive cash inflow.
option_C: An opportunity cost is identical to a nonrefundable historical cost.
option_D: Evaluate the expected incremental value of finishing instead of relying on irrecoverable effort.
rationale: Past irreversible effort is not itself a benefit of future continuation, though remaining alternatives matter.
source_citation: Arkes and Blumer (1985), The Psychology of Sunk Cost, https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Sunk Cost in a decision-making context.
prompt: A lab has paid 900 nonrefundable units for equipment. Completing a project costs 75 more for only 50 in expected future benefit. What is its incremental net value?
option_A: +825 units because the earlier purchase is an asset
option_B: +50 units because future costs should be ignored
option_C: −25 units; completion is not justified on the stated incremental payoff alone
option_D: −925 units because historic expenses must be counted again
rationale: For the continuation decision, 50 − 75 = −25; the 900 is already sunk under the stated assumptions.
source_citation: Arkes and Blumer (1985), The Psychology of Sunk Cost, https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Framing in a decision-making context.
prompt: Two descriptions of an identical program emphasize jobs saved versus jobs lost. What best characterizes a possible framing effect?
option_A: The jobs must have different salaries under the two descriptions.
option_B: An equivalent description always produces identical preferences for every person.
option_C: Choice may depend on the wording despite equivalent underlying consequences.
option_D: Only a change in the underlying probability can alter choice.
rationale: Equivalent outcome representations may lead to different preferences when the emphasized frame changes.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1981), The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7455683

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Framing in a decision-making context.
prompt: A trial reports 18 failures among 90 participants, with no other outcome categories. What is the success percentage?
option_A: 80% succeeded
option_B: 18% succeeded
option_C: 90% succeeded
option_D: 20% succeeded
rationale: There are 72 successes out of 90, so the equivalent success description is 80%.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1981), The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7455683

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Heuristics in a decision-making context.
prompt: An investor hears about several dramatic market crashes and judges crashes more frequent than the long-run record suggests. Which shortcut fits?
option_A: A complete frequency computation from all historical observations.
option_B: Availability, because striking incidents are easily recalled when frequency is estimated.
option_C: A requirement that the actual market crash rate has increased.
option_D: An irreversible expenditure that changes future investment returns.
rationale: Recent vivid crash stories can make extreme events easier to recall without changing their underlying base rate.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Heuristics in a decision-making context.
prompt: A hospital worker estimates a rare complication from a single recent case. Which check reduces availability-based error?
option_A: Give every recent case a probability of one.
option_B: Avoid consulting any historical procedure counts.
option_C: Use a single unrelated patient story as the representative sample.
option_D: Compare observed complications with the total number of comparable procedures.
rationale: The numerator and comparable exposure denominator provide a more defensible estimate than vivid recall.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Prospect Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: An investor describes a portfolio ending at 110 as disappointing after expecting 120 but satisfying after expecting 100. What accounts for the difference?
option_A: The portfolio’s final value must have changed between descriptions.
option_B: The outcome changes sign relative to the chosen expectation reference.
option_C: Reference expectations are excluded from prospect theory.
option_D: The value of any outcome is independent of its reference level.
rationale: With a final value fixed at 110, expectations of 120 and 100 yield a relative loss and a relative gain respectively.
source_citation: Kahneman and Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory, https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Prospect Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A bonus of 115 units is evaluated against a promised 100-unit baseline. What reference-relative change is coded?
option_A: A 100-unit loss
option_B: A 115-unit disappointment
option_C: A 15-unit gain
option_D: No change from the baseline
rationale: The stated difference is 115 − 100 = +15.
source_citation: Kahneman and Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory, https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Nudge Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A cafeteria places healthier items at eye level while selling the same full menu. Why may this count as choice architecture?
option_A: Customers are prohibited from purchasing other menu items.
option_B: The arrangement mathematically changes the calories of every food.
option_C: The intervention always improves well-being for every individual.
option_D: The presentation may influence selection while keeping the original options available.
rationale: Salience and placement can affect choices without removing options; benefits must still be assessed.
source_citation: Thaler and Sunstein (2008), Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness, Yale University Press, ISBN 9780300122237

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Nudge Theory in a decision-making context.
prompt: A school proposes an automatic but reversible email reminder. Which implementation best preserves student autonomy?
option_A: Explain the default and provide a visible, simple way to unsubscribe.
option_B: Send messages regardless of explicit objections.
option_C: Hide all notification settings from recipients.
option_D: Treat silence as permission to remove access to services.
rationale: Transparency and easy reversal preserve choice; privacy and consent requirements remain.
source_citation: Thaler and Sunstein (2008), Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness, Yale University Press, ISBN 9780300122237

learning_objective: Remember: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: In a simple expected-utility model, what is the value of a lottery with outcomes indexed by i?
option_A: The largest possible monetary payoff only.
option_B: The average payoff squared.
option_C: The lowest outcome utility regardless of probability.
option_D: The sum of each outcome utility multiplied by its probability.
rationale: Expected utility is probability-weighted utility, not necessarily expected money.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: Two agents value the same risky cash payoff differently. Which explanation fits expected-utility theory? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
option_A: Probability has no effect on preferences.
option_B: Any preference for certainty proves probability neglect.
option_C: Utilities can represent different preferences over risky outcomes.
option_D: Both agents must maximize expected cash.
rationale: Expected monetary payoff and expected utility can rank lotteries differently.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: An agent has U($0)=0 and U($100)=10. What is expected utility of a 50%-50% lottery over those outcomes? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
rationale: Weight the stated endpoint utilities by probability; both examples evaluate to 5.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Analyze: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: Lottery A gives utility 6 for sure. Lottery B gives utility 10 with probability 0.5 and utility 0 otherwise. Which is preferred under expected utility?
option_A: The certain option: 6 exceeds the gamble’s expected utility of 5.
option_B: The gamble because 10 is its highest payoff.
option_C: Both options because probabilities cancel.
option_D: Neither can be compared without monetary units.
rationale: The expected utility of the equal-probability gamble is 5.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Evaluate: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: A report claims a choice is irrational solely because its expected cash reward is lower. What is the strongest critique?
option_A: Expected utility depends on preferences over outcomes, not just expected cash.
option_B: Expected cash must be maximized in all decision models.
option_C: Utility always equals cash.
option_D: Risk preferences never affect a comparison.
rationale: Without specifying utility, expected-money maximization is not an appropriate universal benchmark.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Create: correctly reason about Utility in a decision-making context.
prompt: Which design best tests whether two learners have different utility curvature?
option_A: Ask whether the learner likes mathematics.
option_B: Offer several choices between sure amounts and probability-defined lotteries, with consistent stakes.
option_C: Ask only for the largest imaginable prize.
option_D: Show an unlabeled picture of a coin.
rationale: Multiple documented sure-versus-risky tradeoffs can help characterize preferences, subject to experimental limitations.
source_citation: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), Princeton University Press; expected-utility framework

learning_objective: Remember: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: Which statement defines loss aversion in reference-dependent choice?
option_A: All losses have exactly zero subjective value.
option_B: The decision maker always dislikes every gamble.
option_C: Only absolute wealth matters, never a reference point.
option_D: A loss can have greater psychological impact than an equal-sized gain.
rationale: Loss aversion compares the subjective impacts of gains and losses around a reference point.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: Why might someone demand more to give up a mug they own than they would pay to acquire it? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
option_A: The market price must have increased.
option_B: The person must be unable to understand money.
option_C: Giving it up may be coded as a loss relative to ownership.
option_D: Ownership makes the mug objectively more useful to everyone.
rationale: Reference-dependent loss aversion is one possible mechanism; other explanations remain possible.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: A commuter views a $10 fee as a loss but a $10 discount as a gain. Which manipulation changes reference dependence? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
option_A: Change both the money and the product quality.
option_B: Remove the reference point from the analysis.
option_C: Assume all participants assign identical utilities.
option_D: Keep final monetary outcomes equivalent while changing the reference description.
rationale: Isolate reference framing while holding actual outcomes constant.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Analyze: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: A seller asks $40 to surrender a ticket but would pay $25 to buy the identical ticket. What can be concluded?
option_A: It proves risk neutrality.
option_B: It is consistent with a reference-dependent valuation gap but does not alone prove its cause.
option_C: It mathematically proves all humans are loss averse.
option_D: It shows the ticket changed its intrinsic quality.
rationale: The gap is suggestive but confounds such as transaction costs must be considered.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Evaluate: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: An article calls all dislike of risk loss aversion. Which criticism is most accurate?
option_A: Reference points are irrelevant.
option_B: Loss aversion is identical to mathematical risk aversion.
option_C: Loss aversion concerns asymmetric valuation of losses and gains relative to a reference point.
option_D: Loss aversion requires all choices to be risky.
rationale: Risk aversion and loss aversion are conceptually distinct, although they may coexist.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Create: correctly reason about Loss Aversion in a decision-making context.
prompt: Which study design best isolates the role of ownership as a reference point?
option_A: Randomize initial ownership, hold incentives constant, and compare willingness to give up versus acquire.
option_B: Interview only owners who refuse all trades.
option_C: Alter product quality for each group.
option_D: Treat initial ownership as an objective price increase.
rationale: Randomization and controlled incentives help isolate reference-dependent ownership effects.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1991), Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, https://doi.org/10.2307/2937956

learning_objective: Remember: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: What is anchoring in numerical judgment?
option_A: The final estimate must equal the first number.
option_B: Only the true population mean matters.
option_C: Numerical values can never affect judgment.
option_D: An initial value can pull a later estimate toward it.
rationale: Anchoring is an influence of a salient starting value on subsequent judgment.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Understand: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: Why could two groups estimate different house prices after seeing different starting prices? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
option_A: The starting values can influence later estimates even when not diagnostic.
option_B: All houses have different physical sizes across groups.
option_C: The high anchor reveals the correct answer.
option_D: Random assignment guarantees identical individual answers.
rationale: A randomized anchor can affect numerical judgment even without genuine informational content.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Apply: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: Additional review variant 3: A salary negotiation opens at an unusually high figure. Which precaution reduces anchoring? Explain the decision using the stated assumptions.
option_A: Multiply the opening number by two.
option_B: Ignore all external price evidence.
option_C: Establish an independent evidence-based range before considering the opening number.
option_D: Accept the opening number as a factual estimate.
rationale: Independent benchmarks may reduce reliance on an arbitrary anchor.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

learning_objective: Analyze: correctly reason about Anchoring in a decision-making context.
prompt: One group sees the number 10 and guesses 32; another sees 90 and guesses 65 on the same task. Which interpretation is safest?
option_A: It is impossible to test numerical anchoring experimentally.
option_B: The difference is consistent with an anchoring effect; design and uncertainty still require examination.
option_C: It proves the estimates are both objectively correct.
option_D: The answers demonstrate loss aversion instead.
rationale: Anchor manipulation and outcome differences support a hypothesis only within a valid design.
source_citation: Tversky and Kahneman (1974), Judgment under Uncertainty, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
